title: Personal Finance Essentials
summary: Budget, save, understand interest and debt, learn investing basics and risk, protect yourself from fraud, and set financial goals.
audience: Students, young workers, families and anyone starting to manage money

body.p: Personal finance is how you earn, spend, save and protect money. The starting point is knowing where your money goes. Income is what comes in, such as wages, business profit or allowances. Expenses are what goes out. If expenses are higher than income, you fall into debt.

A popular guide splits after-tax income into needs, wants and savings. With 200,000 a month, 50% for needs is 100,000, 30% for wants is 60,000 and 20% for savings and debt repayment is 40,000. These are only starting points. In a low-income household needs may take far more, and the aim is then to save even a small amount regularly.

list: Write down all income and spending for one month.
Group spending into needs, wants and savings.
Set a limit for each group and track it weekly.
Pay yourself first: move savings out as soon as you are paid.

body.tip: A budget is a plan, not a punishment. Adjust it when your life changes.

body.p: Saving means keeping money for later instead of spending it now. An emergency fund is money set aside for unexpected costs such as illness, a job loss or a repair. A common target is three to six months of essential expenses. If essentials cost 30,000 a month, six months needs 6 x 30,000 = 180,000.

list: Choose safe places that are easy to reach: a bank savings account, a regulated mobile-money savings product, or a savings group you trust.
Check that the institution is licensed and that deposits are protected where possible.
Avoid schemes that promise very high guaranteed returns. They are often scams.

body.p: Start small and be regular. Saving 5,000 every week adds up. Automate transfers so that saving happens before you can spend the money.

body.tip: Keep emergency savings separate from everyday spending so you are not tempted to use them.

body.p: Interest is the price of using money. When you save, the bank pays you interest. When you borrow, you pay interest. Understanding it protects you from expensive debt.

Simple interest is paid on the original amount only. 100,000 at 5% a year for 3 years earns 100,000 x 0.05 x 3 = 15,000. Compound interest is paid on the original amount plus earlier interest, so it grows faster. 100,000 at 8% compounded yearly becomes 100,000 x 1.08 x 1.08 = 116,640 after 2 years.

list: Always ask for the total cost of a loan, not just the monthly payment.
Compare the annual interest rate and all fees.
Borrow for things that help you earn or have lasting value; avoid borrowing for everyday spending.
Pay more than the minimum on expensive debt such as credit cards and informal loans.

body.tip: If you cannot repay a loan, talk to the lender early. Hiding makes things worse.

body.p: Investing means putting money to work to earn a return over the long term. Returns are never guaranteed, and higher potential returns come with higher risk. Never invest money you may need soon or money you cannot afford to lose.

list: Savings and fixed deposits: low risk, modest returns.
Government and corporate bonds: lend money in return for interest.
Shares: part-ownership of companies; prices rise and fall.
Funds: pooled money managed by professionals, which spreads risk.
Property and business: can pay well but need time, money and knowledge.

body.p: Diversification means spreading money across different investments so one failure does not wipe you out. Inflation, the general rise in prices, reduces the buying power of money, so savings that earn less than inflation lose value over time.

body.tip: Be wary of anyone who promises guaranteed high returns, pressures you to decide fast, or asks you to recruit others. This is a classic scam pattern. This course is general education, not personal financial advice.

lessons.title: Insurance, fraud and protecting your money

body.p: Insurance shares risk. You pay a small regular premium, and the insurer pays for a large loss, such as hospital costs, a house fire or the death of a breadwinner. Choose cover that matches real risks, read what is excluded, and keep records.

list: Never share your PIN, password or one-time code with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank.
Be suspicious of unexpected messages with links, prizes or urgent requests.
Check that lenders and investment platforms are registered with your national regulator.
Keep receipts and agreements in writing.

body.p: Make a will or at least write down your wishes and keep important documents in a safe, known place. Tell a trusted person where to find them.
Review your insurance and your important documents once a year, and update beneficiaries and contact details whenever your family situation changes.

lessons.title: Setting goals and making a plan

body.p: Financial goals give your money a purpose. Make them specific, measurable and time-bound. Saving 120,000 in 12 months for school fees is clearer than 'save more'. Divide the goal by the months: 120,000 ÷ 12 = 10,000 a month.

Review your plan every month. Check what you spent, what you saved and whether your goals are still the right ones. If a goal slips, adjust the amount or the date instead of giving up. Small wins build the confidence to keep going.

list: List your goals and rank them: urgent, medium, long term.
Build a small emergency fund first.
Clear expensive debt.
Save for goals and invest for the long term.
Review monthly and adjust.

body.p: Habits matter more than big decisions. Spend less than you earn, avoid impulse purchases by waiting a day before buying, and keep learning. Teach children about money early.

body.tip: Write down your goal and put it where you see it daily.
